## Findings by module

### camping-basics-1

- **confirmed** (ch-006.txt): SOAC Part 5 wild camping: access rights extend to wild camping that is lightweight, in small numbers and for only two or three nights in any one place; do not camp in enclosed fields of crops or farm animals; keep well away from buildings, roads and historic structures; avoid disturbing deer stalking or grouse shooting; ask the owner's permission to camp close to a house or building; leave no trace by removing litter, all traces of the pitch and of any fire, and causing no pollution. Matches the course; the statutory text adds 'keep well away from roads' and the stalking and shooting caution.
- **refined** (ch-006.txt): SOAC Part 5 human waste: urinate at least 30 m from open water, rivers and streams; defecate as far as possible from buildings, open water and farm animals, and bury faeces in a shallow hole and replace the turf. The course quotes the 30 m rule; the Code's burial instruction is a shallow hole with the turf replaced.
- **refined** (ch-006.txt): SOAC Part 5 lighting fires: use a stove rather than an open fire wherever possible; if you light one, keep it small, under control and supervised, and you might be liable for damage if it escapes; never light one in prolonged dry periods or in forests, woods, farmland, on peaty ground, near buildings or on cultural heritage sites; remove all traces before leaving. Adds 'farmland', 'peaty ground' and liability to the course's fire guidance.
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): SOAC Part 1-2: access rights come from the Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003 and exist only if exercised responsibly; three principles (respect the interests of other people, care for the environment, take responsibility for your own actions); the Code has evidential status before a Sheriff but breaking it is not of itself an offence; rights apply day or night and explicitly include wild camping as a recreational purpose.
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): SOAC 2.11: access rights do not apply on land with a house, caravan or tent, plus enough adjacent land for privacy; farm buildings and yards; land where crops are sown or growing (field margins and unsown ground are fine); sports pitches in use; school land; places charging entry; building sites, railways and quarries; and land exempted by local authority order or covered by byelaws. Also excluded: hunting, shooting, fishing, motorised recreation, and anyone with a dog not under proper control. Gives the course the full list of no-camp ground in Scotland.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): SOAC 3.14-3.20 privacy and night: there are no access rights on 'sufficient adjacent land' next to a house, caravan or tent, normally the garden; keep a sensible distance and avoid ground overlooking a house; at night keep away from buildings where people would not expect anyone, use paths, and remember residents may be fearful and hazards are less obvious. A tent gets the same privacy protection, so do not pitch on top of another camper.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): SOAC 3.24-3.28, 3.38: keep a safe distance from land work, follow reasonable signs during crop spraying (fields can be closed from a few hours up to four days after sulphuric acid spraying) or tree felling, do not climb on bales or timber stacks; leave gates as you find them, climb a locked gate at the hinged end, cross walls and fences near posts or the strongest point; do not park in front of field entrances.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): SOAC 3.47-3.52: take extra care in sensitive habitats (riverbanks, loch shores, marshes, bogs, mountain tops, steep slopes, coastal dunes) to prevent erosion; do not linger if your presence clearly disturbs a bird or animal; do not camp, light fires or use metal detectors on any cultural heritage site (standing stones, burial mounds, ruins, abandoned settlements, many with a natural look), and take nothing away. Gives pitch-selection rules for Scotland the course does not yet state.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): SOAC Part 5 car parking: access rights do not cover motorised activities, so park without blocking field or building entrances or roads, avoid damaging verges, and use a car park if one is near. Confirms the course's point that car or van camping is outside Scottish access rights.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): SOAC Annex 1: under the Trespass (Scotland) Act 1865 it is an offence to light a fire on or near a private road, on enclosed or cultivated land, or in or near a plantation without the owner's consent; under the Civic Government (Scotland) Act 1982 lighting a fire in a public place so as to endanger people or property or cause alarm is an offence; leaving litter in any public open place and polluting water are offences; driving off road is an offence, though parking within 15 yards of a road is not, which still gives no right to park. Gives the course the legal teeth behind the Scottish fire guidance.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): SOAC Part 6: local authorities and national park authorities can make byelaws and management rules, and exempt land from access rights for up to five days (longer needs consultation and Ministers' consent); ask the local authority access officer or ranger service for detailed advice. Supports the course's 'local byelaws override the general picture' callout, for example in national parks.
- **note** (ch-003.txt): SOAC 3.57-3.64: groups, events and businesses need extra care; the bigger the group or the more regular the use, the greater the risk of unreasonable interference; events needing facilities need the land manager's permission. Relevant to a group camp in the capstone, not to a first solo trip.

### camping-basics-6

- **extended** (ch-002.txt): SOAC 3.29-3.34 farm animals: cows can be inquisitive and may react aggressively to dogs, bulls may protect the herd, sheep usually run but can be aggressive with lambs, horses tend to approach, enclosed deer are aggressive in the rut and with young, pigs can turn aggressive at any time; if a bull or pigs are in a field, use a neighbouring field; never take a dog into a field with lambs, calves or other young; with cattle keep the dog on a short lead (under two metres) or close control, and if cows come at you, keep calm, let the dog go and take the shortest safe route out.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): SOAC 3.10-3.12: the outdoors is a working environment and not risk-free; natural hazards include cliffs, steep rocky ground and fast rivers with undercurrents; under the principle 'volenti non fit injuria' a person taking access is generally held to have accepted obvious and inherent risks; take special care for children in your charge. Supports module 6's personal-responsibility framing.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): SOAC 3.53-3.56 dogs: about one in five outdoor visits are with a dog; proper control means no dog in fields with young animals or with vegetables or fruit (unless on a clear path), a short lead (two metres) or close control near cattle, horses and sheep and in ground-nesting areas (moorland, forest, grassland, loch shores, seashore) usually April to July; keep dogs out of water near public supply intakes; a farmer may in some cases shoot a dog attacking livestock; lifting dog faeces in public open places is a legal duty.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): SOAC Part 5 seasonal hazards on Scottish hills: stag stalking usually runs 1 July to 20 October, mostly from August, and normally not on Sundays; use Hillphones or estate signs to find where it is happening and take advised alternative routes; deer control in forests happens all year, often at dawn and dusk; grouse shooting runs 12 August to 10 December, mostly early in the season; tree felling can affect forest roads for months, timber lorries use forest tracks, and children must be kept off timber stacks. Belongs in planning a Scottish wild camp.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): SOAC Part 5 military lands: red flags by day and red lamps at night mark live firing areas that may not be fenced; do not enter when they show; watch for trenches and voids, never pick up objects, and expect sudden loud noises. Also: low-ground shooting (pheasant, partridge, wildfowl) runs in autumn and winter, wildfowling usually at dawn and dusk on the foreshore.
- **note** (ch-007.txt): SOAC 6.12-6.14: if you meet irresponsible behaviour, talk calmly and ask people to explain; never use force; contact the police if behaviour is criminal; report obstructions to the local authority.

### camping-basics-4

- **extended** (ch-002.txt): SOAC 3.34: cow and sheep droppings can carry diseases such as E. coli; the risk is small but most likely if you picnic or camp where farm animals graze or drink water from local streams or burns. Links the pitch choice to water safety: grazed ground and streams below it are the higher-risk case.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): SOAC Part 5 picnicking and litter: avoid picnicking (and by extension cooking or camping) in fields where farm animals are or have recently been, or that have been spread with lime or slurry; take all food scraps and packaging away because animals may eat them and spread disease; bottles, cans and plastic bags can injure or kill animals.
